hops.afterHeading: The map: three checkpoints, two engines
hops.title: How fission yeast mutants got the name wee
hops.text: Paul Nurse never set out to find wee mutants. As a young researcher in Edinburgh in the 1970s, he was hunting fission yeast mutants that grow extra long before dividing. He spun mutated cells through a gradient to collect the big ones and found cells dividing at a small size instead, probably sitting there only because the tiny cells had clumped together. They rushed into mitosis early. The best known had a faulty wee1, the gene for the kinase that holds Cdk1 off with an inhibitory phosphate. Since they turned up in Edinburgh, he called them wee, the Scottish word for small.

sources.citation: Nurse P. Fission yeast cell cycle mutants and the logic of eukaryotic cell cycle control. Mol Biol Cell. 2020;31(26):2871-2873.
Atkin J, Halova L, Ferguson J, et al. Torin1-mediated TOR kinase inhibition reduces Wee1 levels and advances mitotic commitment in fission yeast and HeLa cells. J Cell Sci. 2014;127(Pt 6):1346-1356.

image.caption: Fission yeast with a faulty Wee1 brake divided early and small, so in Edinburgh they were named wee.

hops.afterHeading: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait
hops.title: Seedless watermelon starts with a spindle poison
hops.text: The classic recipe for seedless watermelon begins with a drug that wrecks the spindle. Breeders treat the growing tip of a seedling, which has 22 chromosomes, with colchicine, a poison that, like nocodazole, takes microtubules apart. With no working spindle, the copied chromosomes are never pulled to opposite poles, and the treated shoot can end up with 44. Fertilize that plant with pollen from an ordinary 22-chromosome one, and its seeds grow into plants with 33. Three sets cannot be divided evenly in meiosis, so almost none of its eggs or pollen work. Pollen from an ordinary plant still triggers fruit, which holds mostly soft, empty seed coats.

sources.citation: Singh B, Yun S, Gil Y, Park MH. The Role of Colchicine in Plant Breeding. Int J Mol Sci. 2025;26(14):6743.

Kaseb MO, Umer MJ, Lu X, et al. Comparative physiological and biochemical mechanisms in diploid, triploid, and tetraploid watermelon (Citrullus lanatus L.) grafted by branches. Sci Rep. 2023;13(1):4993.
Wehner TC. Seedless watermelon breeding. Cucurbit Breeding, North Carolina State University.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two laughing children at a sunny picnic table with a halved watermelon and bright red slices that have no black seeds.
image.caption: Colchicine can double a seedling's chromosomes; crossing it with an ordinary plant gives three-set seeds that grow seedless melons.

hops.afterHeading: A worked problem: timing securin destruction
hops.title: Run the half-life math on an afternoon coffee
hops.text: Run the securin math on something you have actually felt: the afternoon coffee. In healthy nonsmoking adults, caffeine's half-life averages about 5 hours, though people range from roughly 1.5 to 9.5. Finish a cup at 3 p.m. and about half its caffeine is still in your body at 8 p.m. A quarter is left at 1 a.m., and an eighth at 6 a.m., around when the alarm goes off. Each half-life removes half of what remains, not a fixed amount, so the last of it lingers longest.

sources.citation: Whitsett TL, Manion CV, Christensen HD. Cardiovascular effects of coffee and caffeine. Am J Cardiol. 1984;53(7):918-922.
Somani SM, Gupta P. Caffeine: a new look at an age-old drug. Int J Clin Pharmacol Ther Toxicol. 1988;26(11):521-533.

audio.title: Elephants, caffeine in a dish, and a Pacific yew
audio.transcript:
Checkpoints can sound like dry wiring diagrams, until you notice where they turn up. Here are three true stories about the brakes in this lesson.

First, elephants. An elephant has far more cells than you do, and it lives for decades. More cells dividing for longer should mean more chances for a cancer to start, so you would expect elephants to get cancer all the time. They don't, and the puzzle even has a name: Peto's paradox. In two thousand fifteen, Lisa Abegglen and her colleagues went through records from six hundred forty-four elephants and estimated that about five percent died of cancer. For people, the estimate is eleven to twenty-five percent. Part of the answer is p fifty-three, the damage responder you met in this lesson. You carry one copy of its gene in each set of chromosomes. African elephants carry at least twenty per set, most of them extra copies made from the original. When the team exposed white blood cells to radiation, about twice as many of the elephant's cells self-destructed as human cells did. An elephant cell with broken D N A, it seems, is more ready to bow out.

Second, a lab trick with caffeine. In nineteen eighty-two, Lau and Pardee damaged the D N A of hamster cells with a chemical. Normally those cells waited in G two for about six hours, and about ninety percent survived. Add two millimolar caffeine, and the G two wait vanished. The damaged cells skipped the repair pause and went straight on into mitosis. Afterwards their nuclei broke into fragments, and the chemical became five to ten times as deadly. For years the explanation looked simple. In nineteen ninety-nine, Sarkaria and colleagues showed that in test-tube assays caffeine blocks A T M and A T R, the upstream kinases that relay the alarm from broken ends and stalled forks. Then in two thousand three, David Cortez found that in living cells given caffeine, those kinases kept signaling, if anything harder than before, and the checkpoint was skipped anyway. The simple story turned into a puzzle. So is your morning coffee switching off your checkpoints? Probably not. As Bode and Dong pointed out in two thousand seven, reaching those dish levels of caffeine in human blood would be extremely difficult without harmful side effects. The dish and the mug live in very different worlds.

Third, a tree. In nineteen sixty-two, on the last day of his collecting trip, U S D A botanist Arthur Barclay took samples from a single Pacific yew in Washington State. It was one of roughly one hundred fourteen thousand plant samples gathered for a National Cancer Institute screen. The bark extract killed cells, and chemists pulled out the active molecule and named it taxol. Colchicine and nocodazole take microtubules apart, so a spindle poison seemed to mean one that dismantles the spindle. In nineteen seventy-nine, Susan Horwitz's lab showed that taxol does the opposite. It helps microtubules assemble and keeps them from coming apart. Either way, the spindle cannot do its job. In one later study, taxol-treated cells stayed in mitosis for at least six hours, held there by Mad two. When the researchers injected an antibody against Mad two, the cells left mitosis after about twelve minutes. Taxol, now called paclitaxel, went on to become an approved treatment for ovarian, breast and lung cancer.

Elephants, caffeine and a yew tree: three reminders that the cell cycle runs on waiting, and that you learn the most about a brake by pressing on it.
